n:
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he heard the words of the sons of Laban, saying.”

*Study note:* The Hebrew word translated “gotten rich” (כָּבוֹד, kavod) has the basic idea of “weight.” If one is heavy with possessions, then that one is wealthy ({{Genesis 13:2|13:2}}). Abraham, Jacob, and Joseph all became wealthy when they left the promised land. Jacob’s wealth foreshadows what will happen to Israel when they leave the land of Egypt ({{Exodus 12:35|Exod 12:35-38}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and from that which belonged to our father he has gained all this wealth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Jacob saw the face of Laban, and look, he was not with him as formerly.” Jacob knew from the expression on Laban’s face that his attitude toward him had changed—Jacob had become *persona non grata*.

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “ancestors” (so NRSV), although the only “ancestors” Jacob had there were his grandfather Abraham and his father Isaac.

*Study note:* *I will be with you*. Though Laban was no longer “with him,” the Lord promised to be.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sent and called for Rachel and for Leah.” Jacob did not go in person, but probably sent a servant with a message for his wives to meet him in the field.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the field.” The word is an adverbial accusative, indicating that this is where Jacob wanted them to meet him. The words “to come to” are supplied in the translation for clarification and stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to his flock.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I see the face of your father, that he is not toward me as formerly.”
*Translator's note:* This rare verb means “to make a fool of” someone. It involves deceiving someone so that their public reputation suffers (see {{Exodus 8:25|Exod 8:25}}).

*Translator's note:* In the protasis (“if” section) of this conditional clause, the imperfect verbal form has a customary nuance—whatever *he would say* worked to Jacob’s benefit.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “speckled” (twice in this verse). The words “animals” (after the first occurrence of “speckled”) and “offspring” (after the second) have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. The same two terms (“animals” and “offspring”) have been supplied after the two occurrences of “streaked” later in this verse.

*Translator's note:* The sentence begins with the temporal indicator, “and it happened at the time of.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the time of the breeding of the flock I lifted up my eyes and I saw.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “going up on,” that is, mounting for intercourse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “said, ‘Lift up (now) your eyes and see.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “going up on,” that is, mounting for intercourse.

*Study note:* *You anointed the sacred stone*. In {{Genesis 28:18|Gen 28:18}} the text simply reported that Jacob poured oil on top of the stone. Now that pouring is interpreted by the Lord as an anointing. Jacob had consecrated the place.

*Study note:* *And made a vow to me*. The second clause reminds Jacob of the vow he made to the Lord when he anointed the stone ({{Genesis 28:20|Gen 28:20-22}}). God is now going to take him back to the land, and so he will have to fulfill his vow.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “arise, leave!” The first imperative draws attention to the need for immediate action.

*Study note:* *Leave this land immediately*. The decision to leave was a wise one in view of the changed attitude in Laban and his sons. But more than that, it was the will of God. Jacob needed to respond to God’s call—the circumstances simply made it easier.
*Translator's note:* The two nouns may form a hendiadys, meaning “a share in the inheritance” or “a portion to inherit.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he devoured, even devouring.” The infinitive absolute (following the finite verb here) is used for emphasis.

*Study note:* *He sold us and…wasted our money*. The precise nature of Rachel’s and Leah’s complaint is not entirely clear. Since Jacob had to work to pay for them, they probably mean that their father has cheated Jacob and therefore cheated them as well. See M. Burrows, “The Complaint of Laban’s Daughters,” *JAOS* 57 (1937): 250-76.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “our money.” The word “money” is used figuratively here; it means the price paid for Leah and Rachel. A literal translation (“our money”) makes it sound as if Laban wasted money that belonged to Rachel and Leah, rather than the money paid for them.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Jacob arose and he lifted up his sons and his wives on to the camels.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “drove away,” but this is subject to misunderstanding in contemporary English.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he led away all his cattle and all his moveable property which he acquired, the cattle he obtained, which he acquired in Paddan Aram to go to Isaac his father to the land of Canaan.”

*Translator's note:* This disjunctive clause (note the pattern conjunction + subject + verb) introduces a new scene. In the English translation it may be subordinated to the following clause.

*Translator's note:* Or “household gods.” Some translations merely transliterate the Hebrew term תְּרָפִים (terafim) as “teraphim,” which apparently refers to household idols. Some contend that possession of these idols guaranteed the right of inheritance, but it is more likely that they were viewed simply as protective deities. See M. Greenberg, “Another Look at Rachel’s Theft of the Teraphim,” *JBL* 81 (1962): 239-48.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stole the heart of,” an expression which apparently means “to deceive.” The repetition of the verb “to steal” shows that Jacob and Rachel are kindred spirits. Any thought that Laban would have resigned himself to their departure was now out of the question.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fleeing,” which reflects Jacob’s viewpoint.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he fled.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he arose and crossed.” The first verb emphasizes that he wasted no time in getting across.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the river”; the referent (the Euphrates) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he set his face.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and it was told to Laban on the third day that Jacob had fled.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his brothers.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he pursued after him a journey of seven days.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “drew close to.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “said to him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “watch yourself,” which is a warning to be on guard against doing something that is inappropriate.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lest you speak with Jacob from good to evil.” The precise meaning of the expression, which occurs only here and in v. {{Genesis 31:29|29}}, is uncertain. Since Laban proceeded to speak to Jacob at length, it cannot mean to maintain silence. Nor does it seem to be a prohibition against criticism (see vv. {{Genesis 31:26|26-30}}). Most likely it refers to a formal pronouncement, whether it be a blessing or a curse. Laban was to avoid saying anything to Jacob that would be intended to enhance him or to harm him.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Jacob pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban pitched with his brothers in the hill country of Gilead.” The juxtaposition of disjunctive clauses (note the pattern vav plus subject plus verb in both clauses) indicates synchronism of action.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you have stolen my heart.” This expression apparently means “to deceive” (see v. {{Genesis 31:20|20}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you have led away my daughters like captives of a sword.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Why did you hide in order to flee?” The verb “hide” and the infinitive “to flee” form a hendiadys, the infinitive becoming the main verb and the other the adverb: “flee secretly.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and steal me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And [why did] you not tell me so I could send you off with joy and with songs, with a tambourine and with a harp?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my sons and my daughters.” Here “sons” refers to “grandsons,” and has been translated “grandchildren” since at least one granddaughter, Dinah, was involved. The order has been reversed in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “There is to the power of my hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “watch yourself,” which is a warning to be on guard against doing something that is inappropriate.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from speaking with Jacob from good to evil.” The precise meaning of the expression, which occurs only here and in v. {{Genesis 31:24|24}}, is uncertain. See the note on the same phrase in v. {{Genesis 31:24|24}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and now.” The words “I understand that” have been supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* The infinitive absolute appears before the perfect verbal form to emphasize the certainty of the action.

*Translator's note:* The infinitive absolute appears before the perfect verbal form to emphasize the degree of emotion involved.

*Study note:* *Yet why did you steal my gods?* This last sentence is dropped into the speech rather suddenly. See C. Mabee, “Jacob and Laban: The Structure of Judicial Proceedings,” *VT* 30 (1980): 192-207, and G. W. Coats, “Self-Abasement and Insult Formulas,” *JBL* 91 (1972): 90-92.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Jacob answered and said to Laban, ‘Because I was afraid.’” This statement is a not a response to the question about Laban’s household gods that immediately precedes, but to the earlier question about Jacob’s motivation for leaving so quickly and secretly (see v. {{Genesis 31:27|27}}). For this reason the words “I left secretly” are supplied in the translation to indicate the connection to Laban’s earlier question in v. {{Genesis 31:27|27}}. Additionally the order of the introductory clause and the direct discourse have been rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for I said.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lest you steal your daughters from with me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “With whomever you find your gods, he will not live.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “brothers.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “recognize for yourself what is with me and take for yourself.”

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause (introduced here by a vav [ו] conjunction) provides supplemental material that is important to the story. Since this material is parenthetical in nature, it has been placed in parentheses in the translation.

*Translator's note:* No direct object is specified for the verb “find” in the Hebrew text. The words “the idols” have been supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he went out from the tent of Leah and went into the tent of Rachel.”

*Translator's note:* The “camel’s saddle” was probably some sort of basket-saddle, a cushioned saddle with a basket bound on. Cf. NAB “inside a camel cushion.”

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause (introduced by a vav [ו] conjunction) provides another parenthetical statement necessary to the storyline.

*Translator's note:* The word “them” has been supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “she”; the referent (Rachel) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let it not be hot in the eyes of my lord.” This idiom refers to anger, in this case as a result of Rachel’s failure to stand in the presence of her father as a sign of respect.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I am unable to rise.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the way of women is to me.” This idiom refers to a woman’s menstrual period.

*Translator's note:* The word “thoroughly” is not in the Hebrew text, but is implied.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it was hot to Jacob.” This idiom refers to anger.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Jacob answered and said to Laban, ‘What is my sin?’” The proper name “Jacob” has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation and the order of the introductory clause and direct discourse rearranged for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “What is my sin that you have hotly pursued after me.” The Hebrew verb translated “pursue hotly” is used elsewhere of soldiers chasing defeated enemies ({{1 Samuel 17:53|1 Sam 17:53}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “what did you find from all the goods of your house?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your relatives.” The word “relatives” has not been repeated in the translation here for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that they may decide between us two.”

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal form indicates that this was a customary or typical action.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from my hand you exacted it.” The imperfect verbal form again indicates that this was a customary or typical action. The words “for every missing animal” are supplied in the translation for clarity; the following clause in Hebrew, “stolen by day or stolen by night,” probably means “stolen by wild beasts” and refers to the same animals “torn by wild beasts” in the previous clause, although it may refer to animals stolen by people. The translation used here, “missing,” is ambiguous enough to cover either eventuality.

*Translator's note:* Or “by drought.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “frost, ice,” though when contrasted with the חֹרֶב (khorev, “drought, parching heat”) of the day, “piercing cold” is more appropriate as a contrast.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my sleep fled from my eyes.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “this to me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “served you,” but in this accusatory context the meaning is more “worked like a slave.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the fear of Isaac,” that is, the one whom Isaac feared and respected. For further discussion of this title see M. Malul, “More on pahad yitschaq ({{Genesis 31:42|Gen. 31:42}}, {{Genesis 31:53|53}}) and the Oath by the Thigh,” *VT* 35 (1985): 192-200.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “My oppression and the work of my hands God saw.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “answered and said.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “daughters.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “children.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but to my daughters what can I do to these today?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cut a covenant.”

*Translator's note:* The verb הָיָה (hayah) followed by the preposition ל (lamed) means “become.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and it will become a witness between me and you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Jacob”; the proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Study note:* The Hebrew word for “pile” is גַּל (gal), which sounds like the name “Galeed” (גַּלְעֵד, galʿed). See v. {{Genesis 31:48|48}}.

*Study note:* *Jegar Sahadutha*. Laban the Aramean gave the place an Aramaic name which means “witness pile” or “the pile is a witness.”

*Study note:* *Galeed* also means “witness pile” or “the pile is a witness,” but this name is Canaanite or Western Semitic and closer to later Hebrew. Jacob, though certainly capable of speaking Aramaic, here prefers to use the western dialect.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a witness between me and you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Mizpah.”

*Study note:* The name *Mizpah* (מִצְפָּה, mitspah), which means “watchpost,” sounds like the verb translated “may he watch” (יִצֶף, yitsef). Neither Laban nor Jacob felt safe with each other, and so they agreed to go their separate ways, trusting the Lord to keep watch at the border. Jacob did not need this treaty, but Laban, perhaps because he had lost his household gods, felt he did.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “between me and you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for we will be hidden, each man from his neighbor.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Laban said to Jacob, ‘Behold this heap and behold the pillar which I have set between me and you.’” The order of the introductory clause and the direct discourse has been rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “This pile is a witness, and the pillar is a witness: surely I will not pass by this pile to you, and surely you will not pass by this pile and this pillar to me, for harm.”

*Translator's note:* *The God of Abraham and the god of Nahor*. The Hebrew verb translated “judge” is plural, suggesting that Laban has more than one “god” in mind. Smr and the LXX, apparently in an effort to make the statement monotheistic, have a singular verb. In this case one could translate, “May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.” However, Laban had a polytheistic world view, as evidenced by his possession of household idols (cf. {{Genesis 31:19|31:19}}). The translation uses “God” when referring to Abraham’s God, for Genesis makes it clear that Abraham worshiped the one true God. It employs “god” when referring to Nahor’s god, for in the Hebrew text Laban refers to a different god here, probably one of the local deities.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by the fear of his father Isaac.” See the note on the word “fears” in v. {{Genesis 31:42|42}}.

*Translator's note:* The construction is a cognate accusative with the verb, expressing a specific sacrifice.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bread, food.” Presumably this was a type of peace offering, where the person bringing the offering ate the animal being sacrificed.

*Study note:* Beginning with {{Genesis 31:55|31:55}}, the verse numbers in the English Bible through {{Genesis 32:32|32:32}} differ by one from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (*BHS*), with {{Genesis 31:55|31:55}} ET = 32:1 HT, {{Genesis 32:1|32:1}} ET = 32:2 HT, etc., through {{Genesis 32:32|32:32}} ET = 32:33 HT. From {{Genesis 33:1|33:1}} the verse numbers in the ET and HT are again the same.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Laban got up early in the morning and he kissed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his sons.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to his place.”

*Study note:* The phrase *angels of God* occurs only here and in {{Genesis 28:12|Gen 28:12}} in the OT. Jacob saw a vision of angels just before he left the promised land. Now he encounters angels as he prepares to return to it. The text does not give the details of the encounter, but Jacob’s response suggests it was amicable. This location was a spot where heaven made contact with earth, and where God made his presence known to the patriarch. See C. Houtman, “Jacob at Mahanaim: Some Remarks on Genesis XXXII 2-3, ” *VT* 28 (1978): 37-44.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Jacob said when he saw them.”

*Study note:* The name *Mahanaim* apparently means “two camps.” Perhaps the two camps were those of God and of Jacob.

*Study note:* *Your servant*. The narrative recounts Jacob’s groveling in fear before Esau as he calls his brother his “lord,” as if to minimize what had been done twenty years ago.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Laban and have lingered until now.”

*Translator's note:* Or “I am sending.” The form is a preterite with the vav consecutive; it could be rendered as an English present tense—as the Hebrew perfect/preterite allows—much like an epistolary aorist in Greek. The form assumes the temporal perspective of the one who reads the message.

*Translator's note:* The words “this message” are not in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “If Esau comes to one camp and attacks it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he said, ‘If Esau comes to one camp and attacks it.” The Hebrew verb אָמַר (ʾamar) here represents Jacob’s thought or reasoning, and is therefore translated “he thought.” The order of the introductory clause and the direct discourse has been rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the surviving camp will be for escape.” The word “escape” is a feminine noun. The term most often refers to refugees from war.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “said.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who said.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will cause good” or “I will treat well [or “favorably”].” The idea includes more than prosperity, though that is its essential meaning. Here the form is subordinated to the preceding imperative and indicates purpose or result. Jacob is reminding God of his promise in the hope that God will honor his word.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the loving deeds and faithfulness” (see {{Genesis 24:27|24:27}}, {{Genesis 24:49|49}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you have done with.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for with my staff.” The Hebrew word מַקֵל (maqel), traditionally translated “staff,” has been rendered as “walking stick” because a “staff” in contemporary English refers typically to the support personnel in an organization.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “this Jordan.”

*Translator's note:* The imperative has the force of a prayer here, not a command.

*Translator's note:* The “hand” here is a metonymy for “power.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for I am afraid of him, lest he come.”

*Study note:* *Heb* “me, [the] mother upon [the] sons.” The first person pronoun “me” probably means here “me and mine,” as the following clause suggests.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “But you, you said.” One of the occurrences of the pronoun “you” has been left untranslated for stylistic reasons.

*Study note:* Some commentators have thought this final verse of the prayer redundant, but it actually follows the predominant form of a lament in which God is motivated to act. The primary motivation Jacob can offer to God is God’s promise, and so he falls back on that at the end of the prayer.

*Translator's note:* Or “will certainly deal well with you.” The infinitive absolute appears before the imperfect, underscoring God’s promise to bless. The statement is more emphatic than in v. {{Genesis 32:9|9}}.

*Translator's note:* The form is the perfect tense with a vav (ו) consecutive, carrying the nuance of the preceding verb forward.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “which cannot be counted because of abundance.” The imperfect verbal form indicates potential here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he took from that which was going into his hand,” meaning that he took some of what belonged to him.

*Study note:* The Hebrew noun translated *gift* can in some contexts refer to the tribute paid by a subject to his lord. Such a nuance is possible here because Jacob refers to Esau as his lord and to himself as Esau’s servant (v. {{Genesis 32:4|4}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he put them in the hand of.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a herd, a herd, by itself,” or “each herd by itself.” The distributive sense is expressed by repetition.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the first”; this has been specified as “the servant leading the first herd” in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to whom are you?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and to whom are these before you?”

*Translator's note:* The form is the perfect tense with the vav (ו) consecutive; it has the nuance of an imperfect of instruction.

*Translator's note:* The words “they belong” have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to your servant, to Jacob.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to my lord, to Esau.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and look, also he [is] behind us.” The referent of the pronoun “he” (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And he commanded also the second, also the third, also all the ones going after the herds, saying: ‘According to this word you will speak when you find him.’”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and look, your servant Jacob [is] behind us.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for he said.” The referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew verb אָמַר (ʾamar), traditionally represents Jacob’s thought or reasoning, and is therefore translated “thought.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will appease his face.” The cohortative here expresses Jacob’s resolve. In the Book of Leviticus the Hebrew verb translated “appease” has the idea of removing anger due to sin or guilt, a nuance that fits this passage very well. Jacob wanted to buy Esau off with a gift of more than 550 animals.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with a gift going before me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will see his face.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Perhaps he will lift up my face.” In this context the idiom refers to acceptance.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the gift passed over upon his face.”

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause is circumstantial/temporal.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he arose in that night and he took.” The first verb is adverbial, indicating that he carried out the crossing right away.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term used here is יֶלֶד (yeled) which typically describes male offspring. Some translations render the term “children” but this is a problem because by this time Jacob had twelve children in all, including one daughter, Dinah, born to Leah ({{Genesis 30:21|Gen 30:21}}). Benjamin, his twelfth son and thirteenth child, was not born until later ({{Genesis 35:16|Gen 35:16-19}}).

*Study note:* Hebrew narrative style often includes a summary statement of the whole passage followed by a more detailed report of the event. Here v. {{Genesis 32:22|22}} is the summary statement, while v. {{Genesis 32:23|23}} begins the detailed account.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he sent across what he had.”

*Study note:* Reflecting Jacob’s perspective at the beginning of the encounter, the narrator calls the opponent simply “a man.” Not until later in the struggle does Jacob realize his true identity.

*Study note:* The verb translated “wrestled” (וַיֵּאָבֵק, vayyeʾaveq) sounds in Hebrew like the names “Jacob” (יַעֲקֹב, yaʿaqov) and “Jabbok” (יַבֹּק, yabboq). In this way the narrator links the setting, the main action, and the main participant together in the mind of the reader or hearer.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “until the rising of the dawn.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* Or “injured”; traditionally “touched.” The Hebrew verb translated “struck” has the primary meanings “to touch; to reach; to strike.” It can, however, carry the connotation “to harm; to molest; to injure.” God’s “touch” cripples Jacob—it would be comparable to a devastating blow.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “dawn has arisen.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he said, ‘I will not let you go.’” The referent of the pronoun “he” (Jacob) has been specified for clarity, and the order of the introductory clause and the direct discourse has been rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Study note:* Jacob wrestled with a man thinking him to be a mere man, and on that basis was equal to the task. But when it had gone on long enough, the night visitor touched Jacob and crippled him. Jacob’s request for a blessing can only mean that he now knew that his opponent was supernatural. Contrary to many allegorical interpretations of the passage that make fighting equivalent to prayer, this passage shows that Jacob stopped fighting, and then asked for a blessing.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he said to him.” The referent of the pronoun “he” (the man who wrestled with Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Study note:* *What is your name?* The question is rhetorical, since the Lord obviously knew Jacob’s identity. But since the Lord is going to change Jacob’s name, this question is designed to focus Jacob’s attention on all that his name had come to signify.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he said.” The referent of the pronoun “he” (the man who wrestled with Jacob) has been specified for clarity, and the order of the introductory clause and the direct discourse has been rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Study note:* The name *Israel* is a common construction, using a verb with a theophoric element (אֵל, ʾel) that usually indicates the subject of the verb. Here it means “God fights.” This name will replace the name Jacob; it will be both a promise and a call for faith. In essence, the Lord was saying that Jacob would have victory and receive the promises because God would fight for him.

*Study note:* *You have fought*. The explanation of the name Israel includes a sound play. In Hebrew the verb translated “you have fought” (שָׂרִיתָ, sarita) sounds like the name “Israel” (יִשְׂרָאֵל, yisraʾel), meaning “God fights” (although some interpret the meaning as “he fights [with] God”). The name would evoke the memory of the fight and what it meant. A. Dillmann says that ever after this the name would tell the Israelites that, when Jacob contended successfully with God, he won the battle with man (*Genesis*, 2:279). To be successful with God meant that he had to be crippled in his own self-sufficiency (A. P. Ross, “Jacob at the Jabboq, Israel at Peniel,” *BSac* 142 [1985]: 51-62).

*Study note:* The name *Perez* means “he who breaks through.” Perez’ birth was surprising because he came out of the womb before his brother Zerah, though Zerah had first reached his hand outside the womb thus being marked as the firstborn. The naming signified the completion of Tamar’s struggle and also depicted the destiny of the tribe of Perez who later became dominant ({{Genesis 46:12|Gen 46:12}} and {{Numbers 26:20|Num 26:20}}). Judah and his brothers had sold Joseph into slavery, thinking they could thwart God’s plan that the elder brothers should serve the younger. God illustrated that principle through these births in Judah’s own family, affirming that the elder will serve the younger, and that Joseph’s leadership could not so easily be set aside. See J. Goldin, “The Youngest Son; or, Where Does {{Genesis 38|Genesis 38}} Belong?” *JBL* 96 (1977): 27-44.

*Study note:* Perhaps the child was named *Zerah* because of the *scarlet thread*. Though the Hebrew word used for “scarlet thread” in v. {{Genesis 38:28|28}} is not related to the name Zerah, there is a related root in Babylonian and western Aramaic that means “scarlet” or “scarlet thread.” In Hebrew the name appears to be derived from a root meaning “to shine.” The name could have originally meant something like “shining one” or “God has shined.” Zerah became the head of a tribe ({{Numbers 26:20|Num 26:20}}) from whom Achan descended ({{Joshua 7:1|Josh 7:1}}).
